The multicenter randomized double-blind phase 3 study included patients with IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma who had progressed on previous therapy. Patients were randomly assigned to Ivosidenib or placebo. Placebo to Ivosidenib crossover was permitted on radiological progression. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival by independent central review. Progression-free survival was significantly improved with Ivosidenib compared with the placebo (median 2.7, vs 1.4 months; hazard ratio 0.37; 95% CI 0.25-0.54; one-side p<0.0001). Median overall survival was 10.8 months for the Ivosidenib group versus 9.7 months for the placebo group (HR 0.69 [95% CI 0.44-1.10]; p=0.060) in which 35 patients were crossover from the placebo group. In a prespecified exploratory analysis, the rank-preserving structural failure time (RPSFT) method was used to reconstruct the survival curve for patients receiving a placebo as if crossover had never occurred. RPSFT assumes that the treatment effect is the same for all patients, regardless of when the treatment is given. The RPSFT-adjusted median overall survival was 6.0 months for the placebo group (HR 0.46 [95% CI 0.28-0.75]; p=0.0008).

DLBCL cell lines carrying the EZH2 Y641N mutation (SU-DHL6 and Karpas422) were used to study the effect of EI1, a selective EZH2 inhibitor that functions by competing with the methyl group donor S-Adenosyl methionine (SAM). Immunoblot assays demonstrated an increase in baseline H3K27me3 and a decrease in baseline H3K27me2 levels in the SU-DHL6 mutated cell line compared to wild-type EZH2 cells. Upon treating cells with EI1, SU-DHL6 cells showed a significant reduction in H3K27me3 and H3K27me2 levels. Gene expression changes in treated Karpas422 cells showed that the early response to EZH2 inhibition is primarily gene up-regulation, consistent with EZH2’s role in transcriptional repression. Ultimately, EI1 treatment led to the down-regulation of a proliferation gene signature and the up-regulation of a memory B-cell signature.

A selective EZH2 inhibitor (EI1) was used to target the EZH2 Y641N mutation in DLBCL cell lines. EI1 treatment significantly inhibited proliferation in EZH2-mutated cells compared to lymphoma cells with wild-type EZH2. When mutated cells were treated with EI1 and examined for DNA synthesis and cell cycle progression, a significant decrease in BrdU+ cells and cells in G2/M was detected, alongside a decrease in cyclin A and B1 levels. Additionally, EI1-treated Karpas422 and SU-DHL6 mutant cells showed a mild increase in the sub-G1 population, and apoptosis was further confirmed in SU-DHL6 cells by the detection of elevated cleaved caspase-3 by western blot. Notably, EZH2 wild-type DLBCL cell lines (such as OCI-LY19, GA10, and Toledo) showed no significant changes in DNA synthesis or cell cycle distribution upon EI1 treatment. These results suggest the Y641N mutation specifically drives cellular proliferation and cell cycle progression in mutated DLBCL cells.

SGC020 was a gastric PDGCX mouse model established from a gastric cancer patient, with a PTEN exon 2-6 gene deletion resulting in undetectable PTEN protein expression. The chemotherapy Taxotere was given at a human equivalent dose of 5 mg/kg weekly. Tumor growth with Taxotere was equivalent to that in mice treated with vehicle control.

A panel of 13 FLT3 tyrosine kinase inhibitors was tested against Ba/F3 cells transfected with FLT3 D835Y using MTT growth/survival assay, and results were compared to Ba/F3 cells transfected with FLT3-ITD. 4 of the TKIs inhibited growth of D835Y cells within 20 fold of concentrations that were effective against FLT3-ITD: Midostaurin (10.0 vs 9.3), Lestaurtinib (9.8 vs 8.6), TTT-3002 (4.1 vs <1.0), and Crenolanib (58 vs 57) nM in D835Y vs ITD.

A panel of 13 FLT3 tyrosine kinase inhibitors was tested against Ba/F3 cells transfected with FLT3 D835Y using MTT growth/survival assay, and results were compared to Ba/F3 cells transfected with FLT3-ITD. 9 of the TKIs were not able to inhibit growth of D835Y cells within the range that authors considered sensitive, which was 20 fold of concentrations that were effective against FLT3-ITD. The TKIs tested that did not meet authors criteria for sensitivity were AG1295, AGS324, Linifanib, Quiz, Sunitinib, Sorafenib, R406, KW2449, and Ponatinib.

In some cancers such as infant ALL, B-lineage ALL and AML samples with the highest levels of wild-type FLT3, constitutive FLT3 phosphorylation is seen from paracrine or autocrine activation from FLT3 ligand FL (FLT3L gene). The authors tested 13 tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) in Ba/F3 cells expressing FLT3, where FL was added to the culture medium to mimic FLT3L autocrine/paracrine activation loops. Crenolanib, R406 and AG1295 were not effective at inhibiting wildtype FLT3 phosphorylation by the author's criteria, having IC50 values greater or equal to 200 nM, which were determined by phospho-FLT3 western blots done at multiple TKI concentrations.

A panel of 13 FLT3 tyrosine kinase inhibitors was tested against Ba/F3 cells transfected with FLT3 D593del using MTT growth/survival assay, and results were compared to Ba/F3 cells transfected with FLT3-ITD. IC50 for Midostaurin, Lestaurtinib, TTT-3002, and Crenolanib against D593del were all within 2x the IC50 for ITD. FLT3-ITD was considered responsive by the authors to each of the TKIs tested. Authors also note that Lestaurtinib, midostaurin, and TTT-3002 inhibited all 10 FLT3 activation loop mutants they tested with similar or even greater strength compared to the FLT3-ITD cells.

Ba/F3 cells with FLT3 D835Y were transplanted into mice. The cells were stably transfected with luciferase and this was used to monitor disease progression with luciferin injections to visualize bioluminescence. After 5 days mice were treated with lestaurtinib, and at 9 days this resulted in greatly reduced leukemic burden in comparison to vehicle controls.

In this phase I study, four Japanese patients with follicular lymphoma were recruited to test the efficacy of EZH2 inhibitor-Tazemetostat. Patients were screened for presence of EZH2 mutations and only one patient had an activating mutation in EZH2. The patients were treated with Tazemetostat at a dose of 800 mg twice a day. Three of the four patients had partial response (including the one with the activating mutation), while one had a stable disease status after the treatment cycle. The authors highlight the treatment's acceptable safety profile and promising antitumor activity in relapsed or refractory B-cell lymphomas.

disease: Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma Germinal Center B-cell Type
evidence_statement: In this phase I study (clinical trial NCT03009344), one patient with germinal center B‐cell‐like (GCB) DLBCL and two with non-GCB DLBCL types were recruited to test the efficacy of EZH2 inhibitor-Tazemetostat in Japanese patients with refractory/relapsed B-cell lymphomas. The patients were treated with a dose of 800 mg twice a day and an objective response was reached only in the patient with the GCB-DLBCL type (complete response), while the other two had progressive disease status. Since EZH2 is known to be expressed in GC and have a role in cellular proliferation and differentiation, the authors speculate that the the cellular origin of DLBCL might be a key in predicting the efficacy of Tazemetostat.

molecular_profile: EZH2 Y646S OR EZH2 Y646F OR EZH2 Y646H OR EZH2 Y646C OR EZH2 Y646N OR EZH2 A692V OR EZH2 A682G
evidence_statement: In this study, Koji Izutsu et al. conducted a multicenter, open-label phase II clinical trial to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the EZH2 inhibitor tazemetostat in Japanese patients with relapsed or refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma harboring activating EZH2 mutations (as detected through the Cobas EZH2 mutations test). Tumor EZH2 mutation status was confirmed using a molecular diagnostic assay (Cobas EZH2 Mutation Test), and patients received oral tazemetostat at 800 mg twice daily in continuous 28-day cycles. The results demonstrated a high level of clinical activity in the follicular lymphoma cohort (n=17), with an objective response rate (ORR) of 76.5%, including 35.3% complete responses and 41.2% partial responses, while the remaining patients had stable disease. Additionally, progression-free survival (PFS) was not reached at a median follow-up of 12.9 months, indicating durable responses. The estimated PFS rate at 12 and 15 months was 94.1% and 73.2%, respectively. In two patients, grade 3 treatment‐emergent adverse event (TEAE) of lymphopenia was seen. While Grade 4 TEAE included hypertriglyceridemia and pneumonia aspiration in one patient, which authors say were not related to tazemetostat. The authors claim treatment was generally well tolerated, with manageable adverse events and no unexpected safety signals. The authors concluded that tazemetostat shows encouraging and durable clinical efficacy with an acceptable safety profile in patients with EZH2-mutant relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma, supporting its use as a targeted therapy for tumors driven by activating EZH2 mutations.

molecular_profile: EZH2 Y646S OR EZH2 Y646F OR EZH2 Y646H OR EZH2 Y646C OR EZH2 Y646N OR EZH2 A692V OR EZH2 A682G
evidence_statement: This phase II study evaluated the efficacy and safety of the EZH2 inhibitor tazemetostat in Japanese adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma harboring EZH2-activating mutations assessed with the cobas EZH2 Mutation Test. Three patients with DLBCL—including two with transformed follicular lymphoma (FL)—who had previously received chemotherapy without available standard therapy, were treated with tazemetostat 800 mg twice daily in 28-day cycles. All three patients achieved an objective response with reduction in tumors from -60 to -80 precent, reaching partial response (PR), although one patient discontinued treatment due to adverse events. In the broader study, 17 patients with relapsed/refractory FL also demonstrated favorable outcomes, with a high objective response rate and manageable safety profile. These results support the clinical activity and tolerability of tazemetostat in EZH2-mutant DLBCL and FL.

molecular_profile: EZH2 Y646S OR EZH2 Y646F OR EZH2 Y646H OR EZH2 Y646C OR EZH2 Y646N OR EZH2 A692V OR EZH2 A682G
evidence_statement: In this large cohort study, 366 patients with follicular lymphoma (FL) were recruited to investigate the incidence and distribution of EZH2 mutations. NGS and Sanger detected EZH2 positive mutations in 101 patients (27.5%). In total, 106 mutations were detected in 101 patients, which included 87 mutations at codon Y646 (Y646N=36, Y646F=27, Y646S=12, Y646H=9, Y646C=3), 9 A682G, and 7 A692V mutations (mean VAF=21.6%). There were 3 novel variants (K634E, V637A and V679M). There was no difference in the mutation frequency at diagnosis (29%; n = 70/237) and relapse (24%; n = 31/129). EZH2 VAFs were compared to other mutation targets to test clonality. Out of the 43 FL tested cases, 81% (35/43) represented true clonal events, while 19% (8/43) were subclonal. For the 33 paired FL and transformed FL (tFL) cases, 8 carried Y646 mutations, and the mutation was maintained in both biopsies in 6 of those cases. Despite no significant association between the mutation status and overall survival of FL patients, authors stress the need to evaluate EZH2 targeted therapy considering the high incidence of EZH2 mutations and their stability during disease progression and/or transformation (tFL).

molecular_profile: EZH2 Y646S OR EZH2 Y646F OR EZH2 Y646H OR EZH2 Y646C OR EZH2 Y646N OR EZH2 A692V OR EZH2 A682G
evidence_statement: In a multicentre, open-label, phase 1 trial, tazemetostat was evaluated in 64 adult patients (≥18 years) with relapsed or refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (n=21) or advanced solid tumours (n=43). Patients received oral tazemetostat in continuous 28-day cycles, with doses ranging from 100 mg to 1600 mg twice daily. The primary objective was to determine the maximum tolerated dose and recommended phase 2 dose, which was established as 800 mg twice daily. Among patients with B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, 8 of 21 (38%; 95% CI: 18.1–61.6) achieved an objective response, with a median time to first response of 3.5 months (IQR: 2.6–6.5). The median duration of response—defined as time until disease progression or death from any cause—was 12.4 months (IQR: 3.5 to >18.3). Tazemetostat was generally well tolerated, with most adverse events being grade 1–2, and dose-limiting toxicities were observed at the highest doses. These results support the clinical activity of tazemetostat in genetically defined populations, including patients with EZH2-activating mutations in B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma and SWI/SNF-deficient advanced solid tumours, providing a foundation for further clinical evaluation in phase 2 studies.

In this phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 514 patients with unresectable stage IIIc–IV, BRAFV600 mutation-positive melanoma were randomly assigned to either 28-day cycles of the atezolizumab, vemurafenib, and cobimetinib group or atezolizumab placebo, vemurafenib, and cobimetinib control group on a 1:1 basis. The trials primary outcome was progression-free survival. It was discovered at the median follow-up of 18.9 months (IQR: 10·4 – 23·8), that progression-free survival was significantly prolonged with atezolizumab versus control (15.1 vs 10.6 months; hazard ratio: 0.78; 95% CI: 0·63 – 0·97; p = 0·025). 13% of patients in the treatment cohort and 16% in the control cohort stopped all treatment due to adverse events.

In this randomized, phase III trial, 572 patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer who had received endocrine therapy previously underwent randomization, including 341 patients with confirmed tumour-tissue PIK3CA mutations. Patients were enrolled into two cohorts based on tumour-tissue PIK3CA mutation status. The comparison was between 300 mg daily alpelisib plus 500 mg fulvestrant every 28 days and once on day 15 versus placebo plus fulvestrant dosed the same. In the PIK3CA-mutated cohort, progression-free survival (PFS) was 11.0 months (95% CI: 7.5 - 14.5) in the alpelisib–fulvestrant group compared to 5.7 months (95% CI: 3.7 - 7.4) in the placebo–fulvestrant group (HR, 0.65; 95% CI: 0.50 - 0.85; p < 0.001). Overall response in the PIK3CA-mutated cohort was greater with alpelisib–fulvestrant than with placebo–fulvestrant (26.6% vs. 12.8%).

molecular_profile: IDH1 R132C OR IDH1 R132H OR IDH1 R132L OR IDH1 R132G OR IDH1 R132S
evidence_statement: This phase 3 clinical trial was conducted to assess the progression free survival in patients with IDH-mutant gliomas treated with Vorasidenib, an oral brain-penetrant inhibitor, which showed preliminary activity in mutant gliomas. In this double-blind study, participants having residual or recurrent IDH-mutated grade 2 gliomas were randomly selected to either receive vorasidenib or placebo in 28-day cycles. The results showed significant improvement in progression-free survival for patients treated with vorasidenib compared to placebo (median progression-free survival, 27.7 months vs. 11.1 months; hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.39; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.27 to 0.56; P<0.001). Vorasidenib treatment also delayed the time to the next intervention.

A phase 1 clinical study conducted with Divarasib in a total of 137 patients, of which 60 patients had NSCLC with G12C mutation in the KRAS gene. Confirmed response was noted in 53.4% (95% CI; 39.9 to 66.7) of the patients, with a progression-free survival of 13.1 months.

molecular_profile: RB1 Wildtype AND ( CDKN2A Loss OR CDKN2A Mutation )
evidence_statement: A phase II clinical study was conducted with 29 patients with Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer harboring CDKN2A alterations and wild-type Rb. The study reported one patient with a partial response, and six patients with SD for a duration of at least 16 weeks. The disease control rate was 31% (90% CI, 19-40). The PFS and OS observed were 8.1 weeks (95% CI, 7.1 - 16.0) and 21.6 weeks (95% CI. 14.1-41.1) respectively. At least one grade 3 or 4 adverse event or serious adverse event was reported in 11 patients, likely associated with palbociclib.

A clinical study in 10 patients with Colorectal Cancer with FLT-3 amplification treated with Sunitinib. Two patients achieved SD, however one of the patients died due to disease progression. A PFS of 10.1 weeks (95% CI; 6.0-15.9) and OS of 38 weeks (95% CI; 7.0 - 47.6) were reported. Overall, no meaningful anti-tumor activity was observed.

This clinical study was conducted with 30 patients with colorectal cancer harboring BRAF V600E (n = 29) or BRAF K601E (n=1) mutations, treated with a combination of cobimetinib and vemurafenib. Of the 30 patients, only 27 were evaluable. An OR rate of 30% (95% CI; 14-50), and DC rate of 52% (95% CI; 35-65) was noted. Eight patients had a partial response with a median duration of 8.1 weeks (5.1-32.3 weeks) and six patients had SD16+ with a median duration of 29.1 weeks (28.1-44.0 weeks). The reported PFS was 15.7 weeks (95% CI; 12.1-18.1) and OS was 38.9 weeks (95% CI; 26.1-49.4). In 43% of the cohort, grade 3 AEs or SAEs were observed, likely associated with the treatment.

This NCI-MATCH trial was conducted in 35 patients of which 29 were included in the primary efficacy analysis with tumors with BRAF V600E mutations, and treated with a combination of dabrafenib and trametinib. The ORR was 37.9% (90% CI, 22.9-54.9). The median PFS and median OS were 11.4 months (90% CI, 8.4-16.3) and 28.6 months respectively. Meaningful results were achieved with this treatment with an overall DCR of 75.9%.

In this NCI-MATCH trial subprotocol Z1F, of the 35 patients enrolled harbouring PIK3CA mutations in their tumors, 25 were included in the primary efficacy analysis and treated with copanlisib. Patients with KRAS mutations were excluded. The ORR was 16% (90% CI; 6-33; p-value = 0.0341), and the clinical benefit rate (complete response, SD or PR for ≥ 6 months) was 36% (90% CI; 20-54). The 6-month PFS rate and PFS were 38% (90% CI; 22-53) and 3.4 months (90% CI; 1.8-6.6) respectively. The OS was 5.9 months (90% CI; 4.9-13.7).

In this phase II NCI-MATCH trial subprotocol I, 61 patients harbouring activating PIK3CA mutations were treated with taselisib. The cohort didn't include any patients with breast or squamous cell lung carcinoma, or patients harboring KRAS or PTEN mutations. No complete responses or PRs were observed in the cohort, the best response being SD in 52% of the patients. The six-month PFS rate was 19.9% (90% CI; 12-29.3), and the PFS was 3.1 months (90% CI; 1.8-3.7). The six-month OS rate was 60.7% (90% CI; 49.6-70), and the OS was 7.2 months (90% CI; 5.9-10.0). Overall, the study reported very limited activity of taselisib in patients with PIK3CA mutations and concluded that the presence of PIK3CA mutation alone is not a sufficient predictor of the drug's activity.

molecular_profile: BRAF V600E OR NRAS Mutation OR HRAS Mutation OR KRAS Mutation OR NF1 Mutation
evidence_statement: In this phase II study of the arm E of the NCI-COG pediatric MATCH trial, 20 patients (median age: 14) were treated with Selumetinib. High-grade glioma (n=7) and rhabdomyosarcoma (n=7) were the most common types of cancers in this cohort. There was no objective response (PR or CR), the best overall response being SD, in three patients. The 6-month PFS rate was 15% (95% CI; 4-34). 25% of the patients had grade 3 or higher AEs, possibly attributed to selumetinib treatment.

molecular_profile: BRAF V600E OR NRAS Mutation OR HRAS Mutation OR KRAS Mutation OR NF1 Inactivating Mutation
evidence_statement: In this Phase II study, 20 patients harboring activating RAS gene mutations (KRAS = 8, NRAS = 3. HRAS = 1), BRAF V600E mutations, and NF1 inactivating mutations (n=7) were treated with Selumetinib. No objected response was reported in these patients, and the six-month PFS was 15% (95% CI; 4-34). 25% (n=5) of the patients experienced a grade 3 or higher adverse effects, likely associated with selumetinib. Overall, selumetinib had limited efficacy in this cohort.

In this trial involving 500 patients, 188 individuals received treatment with VEGF/VEGFR inhibitors. Among them, 106 patients had tumors containing TP53 mutations. The analysis revealed a higher rate of overall improvement, encompassing stable disease (SD), partial remission (PR), and complete remission (CR), at 31% for those treated with VEGF/VEGFR inhibitors compared to 7% for those who didn't receive such treatment. Among patients treated with VEGF/VEGFR inhibitors, those with TP53 mutations (compared to wildtype TP53) exhibited a notably higher rate of improvement, suggesting a sensitivity to this treatment regimen.

In this trial, 19 patients with pediatric brain tumours (1 patient with Astrocytoma, 1 with Fibrillary Astrocytoma, 10 with Pilocytic Astrocytoma, 5 with Ganglioglioma and 2 with Pleomorphic Xanthoastrocytoma) harbouring BRAF V600E were treated with vemurafenib. The study reported a positive response to the treatment, with 1 complete response, 5 partial responses, and 13 patients with stable disease.

In this ongoing phase 2 trial (FIREFLY-1), 76 patients, aged 6 months to 25 years, with pediatric low-grade glioma harbouring BRAF alterations (BRAF fusions or BRAF V600E mutations) were treated with tovorafenib (DAY-101). The overall response rate according to the RAPNO-LGG criteria was 51% (95% CI; 40-63) and the median PFS and DOR were 13.8 months (95% CI; 8.3-16.9) and 13.8 months (95% CI; 11.3 - NR) respectively. All patients experienced at least one adverse event which may be treatment-emergent, and 63% of the patients experienced Grade ≥3 adverse events.

molecular_profile: PIK3CA Mutation OR PTEN Mutation OR AKT1 Mutation
evidence_statement: In a phase 3 trial (NCT04305496) of 708 patients with advanced HR+ HER2- breast cancer, the combination of the AKT inhibitor capivasertib and the estrogen receptor degrader fulvestrant resulted in significantly longer progression-free survival compared to fulvestrant alone. Among the 289 patients (40.8%) with alterations (including PIK3CA, AKT1, or PTEN alterations), the median progression-free survival was 7.3 months in the capivasertib–fulvestrant group compared to 3.1 months in the placebo–fulvestrant group with a hazard ratio of 0.50 (95% CI, 0.38 to 0.65). In the capivasertib–fulvestrant group, 110 patients had PIK3CA mutations, 18 had AKT mutations, 21 had PTEN alterations, 2 had PI3KCA and AKT1 double mutations, and 4 had both PIK3CA and PTEN alterations. A breakdown of response by individual mutation was not provided.

In this phase 2 clinical trial, the efficacy of RAF inhibitor tovorafenib (DAY-101) was investigated in patients between the ages of 6 months and 25 years, with pediatric low-grade gliomas harbouring BRAF alterations (fusions, rearrangements, or V600 mutations). The trial had two arms, arm 1 (n = 77) tested the efficacy of tovorafenib, while arm 2 (n=60) was an extension cohort, which provided treatment access for patients with RAF altered pLGG after arm 1 closure. The RANO-HGG criteria was used to assess efficacy in patients in arm 1. The overall response rate was 67% (95% CI; 54-78). Specifically, 12 (17%) patients had a complete response, 34 (49%) patients experienced a partial response, and 18 (26%) patients had stable disease as the best response. The ORR in patients with BRAF fusions and BRAF V600E mutations was 69% (95% CI; 56-81) and 50% (95% CI; 19-81) respectively. A relatively higher ORR was noted in patients who had received prior MAPK therapy compared to patients who hadn't received prior MAPK therapy. Specifically, the ORR was 71% (95%CI; 54-84) in patients who had received prior MAPK therapy, and 61% (95% CI; 41-78) in patients who hadn't received prior MAPK therapy. The median PFS reported was 19.4 months (95% CI; 16.9 - NR).

In this phase 1/2 clinical trial, 55 patients (40 MDS, 11 AML, 4 MDS/myeloproliferative neoplasms) with myelodysplastic syndromes harbouring TP53 mutations were treated with a combination of eprenetapopt and azacitidine. The ORR was 71% , with 44% achieving complete response. The study reported that patients harbouring only TP53 mutations, and no other somatic mutations by NGS, had higher rates of complete response (69% v 25%; p = 0.006). Overall, the combination therapy of eprenetapopt and azacitidine demonstrated clinically relevant benefits in patients with MDS and AML carrying TP53 mutations.

In this phase 3 double-blind trial, the efficacy of capivasertib and fulvestrant combination therapy was tested in 708 patients with HR+/HER2- breast cancer. Among these 708 patients, 40.8% (n = 289) harboured AKT pathway alterations. The control group received a placebo plus fulvestrant. The median PFS in the population with AKT pathway alterations for the capivasertib-fulvestrant group was 7.3 months compared to 3.1 months in the placebo-fulvestrant group (HR - 0.50; 95% CI [0.38-0.65], p<0.001). In the capivasertib–fulvestrant group, 110 patients had PIK3CA mutations, 18 had AKT mutations, 21 had PTEN alterations, 2 had PI3KCA and AKT1 double mutations, and 4 had both PIK3CA and PTEN alterations. A breakdown of response by individual mutation was not provided.

molecular_profile: PIK3CA Mutation OR RB1 Mutation OR ESR1 Mutation
evidence_statement: In this phase III trial (PALOMA-3), patients with ER+, HER2- advanced breast cancer were treated with CDK4/6 inhibitors. Patients were randomized to receive palbociclib plus fulvestrant (P+F) or placebo plus fulvestrant (F). A paired ctDNA exome sequencing was conducted to analyze clonal composition. RB1 mutations were identified in 6/127 patients (p=0.041), part of the P + F arm, while no RB1 mutations were identified in the patients treated with fulvestrant alone, at EOT (end of treatment). ESR1 mutations were noted in 25.1% at day 1, and 31.3% of the patients at EOT. An increased proportion of PIK3CA mutations were noted at EOT compared to day 1 (19% v/s 26.7%; p = 0.00069). Additionally, the proportions of patients with new PIK3CA mutations did not differ between the two treatment groups, which suggests that these mutations may play a role in fulvestrant resistance. Strong evidence was reported for positive selection for ESR1 Y537S through the treatment in both treatment groups (p=0.0037), suggesting this mutation may promote resistance to fulvestrant. The data also indicates that resistance to fulvestrant may be a major genetic driver of resistance to the combination treatment.

The efficacy of adagrasib + cetuximab combination therapy was tested in 94 patients harbouring colorectal cancers with KRAS G12C mutations. ORR was used as the primary end-point for the study. The ORR and disease control rate were 34.0% and 85.1% respectively. The median duration of response and progression free survival were 5.8 months (95% CI; 4.2-7.6). and 6.9 months (95% CI; 5.7-7.4) respectively. The overall survival was 15.9 months (95% CI; 11.8-18.8).

In this trial, patients with advanced rare tumours harbouring BRAF V600E mutations were treated with a combination of dabrafenib and trametinib. The study included eight distinct cohorts: anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) (n=36), biliary tract cancer (BTC)(n=43), gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) (n=1), adenocarcinoma of the small intestine (ASI) (n=3), low-grade glioma (LGG) (n=13), high-grade glioma (HGG)(n=45), hairy cell leukemia(HCL) (n=55), and multiple myeloma (MM)(n=19). The overall response rates for these cohorts were 56%, 53%, 0%, 67%, 54%, 33%, 89%, and 50% respectively. The median duration of response varied, with 14.4 months for anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, 8.9 months for biliary tract cancer, 7.7 months for adenocarcinoma of the small intestine, 31.2 months for high-grade glioma, and 11.1 months in multiple myeloma. In the remaining cohorts, the duration of response was not reached. Progression-free survival was measured at 6.7 months for ATC, 9.0 months for BTC, 9.5 months for ASI, 5.5 months for HGG, and 6.3 months for MM. PFS could not be evaluated in the LGG and HCL groups due to small patient numbers. The overall survival was 14.5 months for ATC, 13.5 months for BTC, 17.6 months for HGG, 21.8 months for ASI, and 33.9 months for MM cohorts. OS could not be evaluated for the LGG and HCL groups due to a low number of deaths. Adverse events were reported in 97.6% of the patients (n=201), with 87.9% (n=181) of these being related to the study treatment. Serious adverse events occurred in 45.1% (n=93) of patients across all cohorts.

In this trial, patients with pediatric (age <18 years) low-grade gliomas harbouring BRAF V600E (n=49), were treated with either trametinib monotherapy (n=13) or dabrafenib + trametinib (n=36). In patients treated with trametinib monotherapy, 15% (95% CI, 1.9-45.4; n=2) had objective PRs, and 46% (n=6) had stable disease for 12 or more weeks after the first dose of therapy. The estimated 24-month duration of response (DOR) was 100%. The median PFS was 16.4 months (95% CI, 3.2 to NR). In patients treated with a combination of trametinib and dabrafenib 25% (95% CI, 12.1-42.2; n=9) had objective PRs and 64% (n=23) experienced stable disease. The median DOR was 33.6 months (95% CI, 11.2 - NR), while the 24-month DOR was 80% (95% CI, 30-100). The median PFS was 36.9 months (95% CI, 36.0 - NR).

In this phase 3 trial, patients with chemorefractory metastatic colorectal cancer harbouring KRAS G12C mutations were assigned to one of three groups. The first group received 960 mg of sotorasib (KRAS G12C inhibitor) once daily plus panitumumab (n = 53), the second group received 240 mg of sotorasib once daily plus panitumumab (n=53), and the third group received investigator's choice of trifluridine-tipiracil or regorafenib/standard-care (n=54). The median PFS was 5.6 months (95% CI, 4.2-6.3) in the 960-mg sotorasib-panitumumab, 3.9 months (95% CI, 3.6-5.7) in the 240-mg sotorasib-panitumumab, and 2.0 months (95% CI, 1.9-3.9) in the standard care group. The hazard ratio for disease progression or death compared to the standard care cohort was 0.48 (95% CI, 0.30-0.78, p=0.005) in the 960-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group and 0.59 (95% CI, 0.37-0.95, p=0.036) in the 240-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group. The ORR was 26.4% (95% CI, 15.3 to 40.3), 5.7% (95% CI, 1.2 to 15.7), and 0% (95% CI, 0.0 to 6.6) in the 960-mg sotorasib–panitumumab, 240-mg sotorasib–panitumumab, and standard-care groups, respectively. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse effects occurred in 35.8% of the 960-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group, 30.2% of the 240-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group, and 43.1% in the standard care group. Overall, the study concluded that the 960-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group resulted in a longer PFS compared to the standard treatment, and toxic effects were expected with limited discontinuation.

The study demonstrates that EZH2 A677G is a gain-of-function mutation in B-cell lymphoma. In enzymatic assays, A677G uniquely utilized unmethylated, monomethylated, and dimethylated substrates with nearly equal efficiency. Structural modeling indicated that the A677G mutation enlarges the lysine tunnel to accommodate dimethylated substrates, while retaining the crucial Y641 residue for orienting unmethylated and monomethylated substrates. To evaluate its biological effect, the authors transiently expressed A677G in wild-type EZH2 MCF-7 cells, which resulted in marked global increases in H3K27me3 levels and a reduction in H3K27me2, relative to wild-type EZH2. These findings support the role of A677G as an activating mutation capable of altering the epigenetic landscape.

molecular_profile: PIK3CA H1047R OR PIK3CA H1047Y OR PIK3CA H1047L OR PIK3CA H1047D OR PIK3CA H1047I OR PIK3CA H1047N OR PIK3CA H1047P OR PIK3CA H1047Q OR PIK3CA H1047T
evidence_statement: The phase III INAVO120 trial (NCT04191499) in 325 patients with endocrine-resistant, PIK3CA-mutated HR⁺/HER2⁻ locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer evaluated inavolisib plus palbociclib and fulvestrant (n=161) versus placebo plus palbociclib and fulvestrant (n=164). Median PFS was 15.0 months (95% CI 11.3–20.5) versus 7.3 months (95% CI 5.6–9.3; HR 0.43; 95% CI 0.32–0.59; P<.0001), with ORR of 58% (95% CI 50–66) and median DOR of 18.4 months compared to 25% (95% CI 19–32) and 9.6 months in the control arm. The most common adverse events (≥20%) included neutropenia, hyperglycemia, stomatitis, diarrhea, and rash, consistent with the PI3Kα inhibitor class. Efficacy outcomes were reported for all eligible PIK3CA mutations detected by the FoundationOne Liquid CDx assay, which covers hotspot mutations in exons 2 (R88, G106, K111, G118), 5 (N345), 8 (C420, E453), 10 (E542, E545, Q546), and 21 (M1043, H1047, G1049); individual patient numbers by mutation were not provided.

evidence_statement: In a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled biomarker-selected adjuvant study (ALASCCA, NCT02647099; colorectal carcinoma; n = 626; group A: PIK3CA exon 9/20, n = 314), aspirin 160 mg daily (group A n = 157) for 3 years reduced colorectal cancer recurrence vs placebo (group A n = 157) in the PIK3CA hotspot subgroup (3-yr cumulative incidence 7.7% vs 14.1%; HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.24 - 0.98; P = 0.04) with 3-yr DFS 88.5% vs 81.4% (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.34 - 1.08). Severe AEs occurred in 16.8% vs 11.6% with events including GI bleeding and subarachnoid hemorrhage, and one out of the 4 observed deaths was deemed possibly related to aspirin; OS at 5 yr was not significantly different (91.6% vs 90.1%; HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.37 - 1.68).

molecular_profile: PIK3CA Mutation OR PTEN Mutation OR PIK3R1 Mutation
evidence_statement: In a randomized, double blind, placebo controlled adjuvant trial in colorectal carcinoma with PI3K pathway mutations (ALASCCA, NCT02647099; group B n = 312), aspirin 160 mg daily (group B n = 156) for 3 years reduced 3 year recurrence vs placebo (n =156) (7.7 percent vs 16.8 percent; HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.21 - 0.83) and improved 3 year DFS (89.1% vs 78.7%; HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.29 - 0.88), while 5 year OS was not significantly different (93.0% vs 89.7% ; HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.30 - 1.51). Severe AEs occurred in 16.8% vs 11.6% with events including GI bleeding and subarachnoid hemorrhage, and one out of the 4 observed deaths was deemed possibly related to aspirin.

molecular_profile: TP53 R273C OR TP53 G245S OR TP53 R213*
evidence_statement: In the phase I study of pazopanib and vorinostat in 36 patients with advanced solid tumors, detection of hotspot TP53 mutation was associated with a higher rate of SD ≥6 months/PR, longer median PFS (months), and longer median OS (months) compared to patients without a hotspot TP53 mutation. In colorectal cancer cases, detected TP53 hotspot mutations included TP53 R213*, TP53 G245S, and TP53 R273C. In the subgroup of patients with metastatic colorectal cancer and sarcoma treated with pazopanib and vorinostat, those with detected hotspot TP53 mutations (n = 6) had a significantly longer median PFS of 6.5 months (95% CI 3.0–9.0; p = 0.023) compared to 2.0 months (95% CI 1.8–2.2; p = 0.023) in TP53-undetected cases (n = 10), and a significantly longer median OS of 19.8 months (95% CI 8.2–31.4; p = 0.021) versus 7.2 months (95% CI 0.6–13.8; p = 0.021), respectively.

An 8-year-old girl presented with secondary BRAF V600-mutant histiocytic sarcoma following T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. After the poor response to initial salvage chemotherapy, the patient responded well to dabrafenib and trametinib combination therapy and remained in partial remission with no disease progression for 3 years.

In this 2020 study, the authors analyzed four cases of follicular lymphoma using circulating tumor DNA and droplet digital PCR to monitor EZH2 hotspot mutations, including A682G. One patient with transformed follicular lymphoma carried the EZH2 A682G mutation with a variant allele frequency of 1.8% in a bone marrow biopsy; seven months later, after multiple failed lines of therapy, the mutation was detected concurrently at 38.2% in a lymph node biopsy and 74.0% in circulating tumor DNA shortly before the patient's death. In this patient, the A682G mutation persisted across multiple anatomical sites and coincided with immunochemotherapy resistance, aggressive transformation, and a fatal disease outcome. Furthermore, the patient's EZH2 mutation levels in circulating tumor DNA tracked with tumor burden and PET-CT findings, suggesting that monitoring the persistent A682G mutation may reflect disease progression and treatment failure. The authors note that activating EZH2 mutations, including A682G, are clinically relevant in follicular lymphoma (occurring in ~25% of patients) and suggest they can serve as biomarkers for tumor burden and disease aggressiveness, supporting an oncogenic association of EZH2 A682G in follicular lymphoma.

In this 2013 study, the authors analyzed 366 follicular lymphoma (FL) patients with additional paired samples from 33 cases of transformed FL. Patients harbored EZH2 mutations predominantly at codons Y646, A682, and A692, with variant allele frequencies (VAFs) ranging from 2% to 61%. In total, 9 A682G mutations were detected. Comparative analysis with other recurrently mutated genes (CREBBP, MLL2, TNFRSF14, and MEF2B) demonstrated that the majority of EZH2 mutations were clonal. Gene expression analysis of high tumor-content samples identified 106 differentially expressed genes associated with EZH2-mutant cases. The authors conclude that EZH2 mutations act as early events in follicular lymphoma and contribute to disease pathogenesis.

This study provides robust preclinical evidence, supported by genomic data from human tumors, demonstrating that exon 4 mutations in KRAS (particularly at codon 146) represent functionally oncogenic variants. Specifically, experimental assays show that these variants increase the active, GTP-bound fraction of KRAS, promote activation of proliferative signaling pathways, and are capable of inducing cellular transformation. In parallel, tumor-derived data indicate that these mutations recur in specific cancer types and display patterns consistent with driver events. However, compared to classical KRAS mutations (codons 12 and 13), these variants exhibit lower levels of activation and reduced transforming capacity, suggesting a distinct mechanism of activation and a more moderate oncogenic potential.
